packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cut exact-minimum payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce debt, because nudged users chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and cash-strapped users disengaged from autopay.
packets.methodology: Randomised field experiment on live credit-card accounts, six-month follow-up.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly undermines the 'defaults always help' premise in a consumer financial product: a nominally successful nudge changed enrolment behaviour without changing the underlying outcome, exactly the 'vanity enrolment' risk support raised.
limitations: credit-card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
effect measured at 6 months only, not 12
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Defaults in wealth-management advice significantly shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (or overriding one) lowers the client's rating of the advice received, an effect mediated by perceived advisor honesty; framing of the default question (how much to invest vs. how much to leave safe) also shifts allocations.
packets.methodology: Three experiments including a large representative sample across five European countries (n=4207) on default and framing manipulations in investment advice.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests, in an EU consumer-financial-advice setting, exactly the manipulation/reputational-risk trade-off the brief flags: a default that shifts behavior can also erode trust, and how the default and preset level are framed changes both compliance and perceived honesty -- this should shape how the round-up multiplier default is presented, not just which value is chosen.
limitations: wealth-management investment advice rather than a round-up savings feature
no persistence data beyond the experimental session
risk-taking outcome, not enrollment/contribution behavior
packets.relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-advice experiment on defaults and framing that directly informs the manipulation/dark-pattern and anchoring questions the brief raises.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with larger effects on smaller and less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across political campaign websites around the 2020 US election.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows a default can move nominal financial commitment (recurring donations) without users intending it, evidenced by elevated refund requests - precisely the 'passively enrolled, didn't understand what they signed up for' failure mode the support team worries about for round-up enrolment.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
US election context, not the EU consumer-protection regulatory setting
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest empirical demonstration that a recurring-financial-commitment default can produce unintended, regretted enrolment, direct evidence for the manipulation/dark-pattern risk the brief flags.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: After the EU Digital Markets Act mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects observed from 15 months after rollout onward.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered rollout of DMA-mandated choice screens on iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly answers whether forced active choice can meaningfully shift outcomes away from an incumbent default in a mobile-app, EU-regulatory setting nearly identical to ours, evidence that active choice's effect persists well past onboarding.
limitations: outcome is browser usage, not financial enrolment or savings amount
platform-level natural experiment, not a within-app active-choice test
packets.relevance_reason: The closest available natural experiment on active choice versus default in an EU-regulated mobile-app setting, directly bearing on the active-choice-vs-default decision.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: Steady-state saving rates increase by only 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% due to default auto-escalation once job turnover, withdrawal on separation, and opt-outs are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalation defaults escalate on the first date.
packets.methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out dynamics.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift from opt-out defaults shrinks dramatically once medium-run attrition and disengagement are modeled, directly bearing on whether an opt-out round-up default would be vanity enrollment.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated context absent from our product
auto-escalation dynamic differs from a fixed round-up multiplier
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrollment reliably raises saving once medium/long-run dynamics are modeled, with numeric effect sizes.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for downstream (post-enrollment) default effects, identifying time course of choice, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators of whether default effects persist or fade.
packets.methodology: Conceptual review and theoretical framework synthesizing prior consumer-behavior findings; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to think about exactly the question the brief raises -- whether default-driven enrollment persists or decays -- and what to measure (antecedent preference strength, trade-off salience) to predict which outcome we'll get.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical, not a specific empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer-behavior framework directly addressing persistence and heterogeneity of default effects, the two open empirical questions in the brief.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Opt-out defaults increased sign-up in both single-exam and many-exam settings, but only translated into greater effortful task completion (participation and passing) for the single, strongly-endorsed default and only among previously responsive individuals; for many exams and non-responsive individuals there was no effect on actual outcomes despite higher sign-up.
packets.methodology: Two field experiments changing university exam sign-up to opt-out, tracking downstream effortful outcomes (participation, passing).
packets.why_it_matters: The most direct evidence available that a default can raise nominal enrolment without increasing the effortful behaviour it's meant to produce unless targeted at people already inclined to engage, exactly the 'passively enrolled users don't engage' concern the support team raises about round-up savings.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial savings product
effort/engagement measured through exam behaviour, not money saved or withdrawn
packets.relevance_reason: Directly tests whether an opt-out default that raises sign-up also raises real engagement, the core mechanism behind the brief's disengagement worry, making it the closest available evidence on that specific question despite the non-financial setting.
packets.title: Defaults and effortful tasks
packets.abstract: Abstract Nothing is known about the effectiveness of defaults when moving the target outcomes requires substantial effort. We conduct two field experiments to investigate how defaults fare in such situations: we change the university exam sign-up procedure in two study programs to “opt-out” (a) for a single exam, and (b) for many exams. Both interventions increase task uptake (exam sign-up). Concerning the outcomes which require effort, we find no effects for many exams. For a single exam, the opt-out increases task completion (exam participation) in the study program where the default arguably entails stronger endorsement. Within this program, the effects on successful task completion (exam passing) are heterogeneous: treated students who in the past were willing to communicate with the university (responsive individuals) invest more effort into exam preparation and are more likely to pass the exam than their control counterparts.For non-responsive individuals, we find increased sign-ups but no effects on the target outcomes. Defaults can thus be effective and may be an attractive policy option even when the target outcome requires substantial effort provision. It is, however crucial that the interventions target the appropriate individuals.

packets.key_finding: At-scale automatic enrolment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts at UK banks cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide.
packets.methodology: Large-scale field experiments run directly inside UK bank consumer accounts.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for auto-enrolling consumers into a banking-app feature by default rather than by choice, in the same consumer-financial, self-directed setting as the round-up feature - evidence that opt-out defaults inside a bank app can produce real financial benefit, not just nominal sign-up.
limitations: measures downstream financial outcomes (overdraft charges) rather than enrolment or contribution-level persistence directly
no comparison against opt-in or active-choice enrolment
packets.relevance_reason: Directly analogous consumer-banking automatic-enrolment field experiment, the nearest real-world precedent to the round-up feature itself.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default conservative fund, with half still anchored on the default after three years.
packets.methodology: Multi-year administrative data analysis from three large US firms comparing automatic versus voluntary 401(k) enrolment.
packets.why_it_matters: Closest prior work directly quantifying anchoring on a preset default contribution level and its persistence over years, the exact evidence needed for the C3 decision on whether to pre-set a round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) plan with employer as trusted intermediary, the mechanism the brief says does not carry over
illiquid long-horizon retirement savings versus liquid round-up sweeps
2001 data predates app-based fintech and current EU regulatory norms
packets.relevance_reason: Closest prior work quantifying both the default-enrolment effect and, specifically, anchoring at a preset contribution level over multiple years — directly informing the multiplier pre-set decision.
packets.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

packets.key_finding: A synthesis of household-finance research covering consumption/savings, choice architecture, product design, and defaults as one of several intervention classes shaping household financial behaviour.
packets.methodology: Narrative review/chapter summarising empirical regularities and behavioural interventions across household finance topics; abstract-only detail here.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the project a synthesis-level view of where defaults and choice architecture sit among other consumer-finance interventions (education, disclosure, product design), useful for weighing default design against non-default levers.
limitations: broad chapter covering many topics, not focused specifically on enrolment defaults for liquid savings
abstract gives no effect sizes
mixes employer-plan and consumer-finance literatures without separating the intermediary distinction the brief flags
packets.relevance_reason: The review/meta-level synthesis the brief asks for, situating default and choice-architecture effects within the broader household-finance intervention literature.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

alternates.key_finding: In an RCT of 220 participants, social-norm, framing, default-option, and positive-narrative nudges all significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings relative to control, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
alternates.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey, 220 participants, testing multiple behavioural nudges including default options on voluntary pension contributions.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that 'defaults will lift enrolment' - here the default nudge backfired and reduced willingness to contribute, with heterogeneity by income, education, gender, and trust, underscoring that context and institutional trust determine whether a default helps or hurts.
limitations: small online-survey sample (n=220) in China, cultural/institutional context differs from the EU
voluntary pension framing rather than a bank-app round-up feature
alternates.relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the set: an RCT where default options actively reduced willingness to save, directly undercutting the premise the brief asks us to test.
alternates.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
alternates.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
alternates.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

alternates.key_finding: A field-experiment reminder nudge cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
alternates.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial-management platform in Brazil; abstract-only for further design detail.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the brief's central worry — a well-intentioned nudge can help most users on average while making a vulnerable subgroup worse off — which should push the team toward monitoring distributional outcomes (e.g. overdraft-prone users) before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies reminder nudges, not enrollment defaults, so it does not directly measure opt-in/opt-out/active-choice effects
credit-card and overdraft context rather than a savings round-up product
abstract gives no long-horizon (6-12 month) persistence data
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides the strongest available consumer-finance evidence on heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, side effects of a well-meaning nudge — exactly the distributional risk (C5) the brief flags as a reason not to default everyone in.
alternates.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
alternates.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: In an opt-in short-term savings program at five U.K. firms, take-up was extremely low (no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account), but among those who did opt in, 96% still held a positive balance and 87% received a payroll contribution at 12 months.
alternates.methodology: Field study of program introduction and administrative account data tracked over 12 months at five U.K. firms.
alternates.why_it_matters: This is the closest prior work to our exact product: a liquid, withdrawable, payroll-linked savings account under opt-in enrollment. It shows opt-in alone yields near-vanishing scale despite strong retention among enrollees -- direct evidence for the entry-design trade-off between enrollment scale (opt-out/active choice) and engagement quality (opt-in) that the brief is deciding.
limitations: enrollment is via employer payroll deduction, not a self-service app, so the channel-to-attention differs
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice conditions in this sample
UK employer context rather than EU consumer app
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest prior work on a liquid, short-term, opt-in savings product, directly quantifying the take-up vs. retention trade-off central to the entry-design decision; the product studied (payroll-linked short-term savings) is far closer to a round-up feature than any retirement plan.
alternates.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
alternates.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.

alternates.key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision with no default) can be strengthened into 'enhanced active choice,' which highlights losses from the non-preferred option, as an alternative to automatic enrolment when opt-out is infeasible or ethically fraught.
alternates.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and a novel enhanced active-choice variant against no-default and default conditions.
alternates.why_it_matters: Supplies the specific mechanism (forced choice plus loss-framed messaging) that the brief's decision 1 is directly choosing between opt-in/opt-out/active choice — a concrete design for capturing enrolment benefit without full auto-enrolment.
limitations: medication-adherence and general behaviour-change settings, not a financial product
no financial-savings outcome measured
field experiments are the studies reviewed rather than a single large trial with a stated effect size
alternates.relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: the active-choice and enhanced-active-choice design tested here is precisely the third entry-design option the brief must decide between, and the loss-framing technique for the non-default option carries directly into UI copy design.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: A representative Australian sample (n=2,100) rated financial nudges positively overall, favoured System-2 (reflective) interventions and savings-framed messaging, and did not find transparency to reduce approval, though manipulation perceptions varied by framing.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment with 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing, and System-1/System-2 targeting; six outcome measures including manipulation and likelihood of bank use.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly tests when a bank-proposed financial default or nudge is perceived as manipulative versus helpful, which is the exact reputational question the EU dark-pattern concern raises for choosing opt-out entry.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios rather than actual product use
Australian sample, not EU
no measurement of actual enrolment or savings behaviour
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides direct consumer-facing evidence on manipulation/approval perceptions of financial defaults, the missing piece for the dark-pattern risk question.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.
